cells.verb: keeping two things alive at once, feeding both instead of choosing
cells.place: where what each one gets is weighed and set right
cells.ask: If you want to, let one person see what the tending has cost you — and set down the one piece that's already finished. What comes back is the ease of putting something down because it's done, not because you gave up.
cells.core: You're keeping two things alive at once, and neither one is starving. When something tips, you adjust the pour rather than picking a winner, and you do it without much noise — which is why people trust how you split things. The fairness here isn't a rule you consult. It's a thing you tend, and it's growing.
cells.sheetLine: You keep both sides fed, and nobody has to lose for it to be fair.

cells.tense: Future — bracing against a shortage that hasn't come.
cells.verb: re-measuring every share against what might run out
cells.place: where what each one gets is weighed and set right
cells.ask: Pick one thing you already set right and let yourself be satisfied with how it turned out — all the way, no footnote, no re-check. What comes back is care that feeds things without emptying you.
cells.core: You're adjusting for a shortfall that hasn't happened. Every allotment gets held up against a future where someone ends up with less, and the measuring never closes — so the care that was meant to feed things is spending itself on checking the scales. Nothing is being left alone long enough to grow.
cells.sheetLine: You're re-balancing against a shortage that hasn't arrived.

cells.tense: Past — standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: letting what's out of proportion sit untended
cells.place: where what each one gets is weighed and set right
cells.ask: Rather than forcing your hands back onto the work, pick one outcome you still want here and say it — to yourself, to someone — and keep saying it after it's gotten hard. What comes back is tending that doesn't feel like forcing.
cells.core: There's something uneven in front of you, and you've stopped tending it. Somewhere back there, trying to keep things fair didn't take — and the hands came off. What's out of proportion is still out of proportion. You're not fighting it; you're just letting it sit where it fell.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped evening things out and started letting them sit.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing.
cells.verb: quietly topping up whichever side is short
cells.place: where what each one gets is weighed and set right
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, one thing you've been going without so the shares stay even. What comes back is being able to hold the balance without having to disappear into it.
cells.core: You're already the one keeping it fair — covering the side that's short, taking the smaller portion so the whole thing stays level — and you'd describe it as just how things happened to work out. The tending is yours. The giving-up is yours too. Neither one has your name on it yet.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping it fair. You've been calling it luck.
